facts.text: The black phoebe is a passerine bird in the tyrant-flycatcher family.
Its song is a repeated tee-hee, tee ho.
Habitats must also include a supply of mud for nest building, and the birds' specialized nesting requirements probably cause their somewhat irregular range.
The phoebe can be recognized by a characteristic "tail-wagging" motion, in which the tail is lowered and the tail's feathers fanned out.
It is mainly insectivorous and waits on a perch before sallying out and catching its prey in the air.
Its song consists of two alternating phrases.
It makes an open cup nest which is placed under a cliff or a bridge and cemented in its place with mud.
It lives in a variety of habitats but is always near water.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 26 cm from its wing length.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in rocky places.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It lays 1 to 6 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the black phoebe never strays from water, and the tale answers: it needs the mud.
Under a cliff or a bridge it builds an open cup and cements it in place with mud.
Then it waits on a perch, and when an insect passes, it sallies out and snatches it from the air.
Back on its perch, it lowers its tail and fans the feathers wide.
So its song rings by the water: tee-hee, tee ho.

tagline.text: The mud builder of the water's edge, waiting on its perch.
